description: Cassiopeia: Five engineers, five stars, infinite possibilities in code and space.
summary:
Fire in microgravity is invisible and deadly, lacking the smoke drift we rely on for early detection on Earth. While NASA possesses over 50 years of combustion data, there is no live intelligence layer to act on it. Enter IGNIS, an SI-powered spacecraft fire safety ecosystem, and Ember, its AI agent.

IGNIS bridges historical data with real-time action by integrating NASA's PSI database with spacecraft cameras using Edge Computer Vision. Ember constantly monitors feeds to detect invisible cool flames and thermal anomalies. When a threat is detected, it instantly triggers multi-channel alarms—alerting astronaut tablets, flashing the dashboard, and sounding station sirens. Beyond detection, Ember acts as an interactive assistant, allowing crew members to ask questions and receive instant, actionable suppression protocols. IGNIS transforms a passive data archive into a proactive, life-saving system for future Moon and Mars missions.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

IGNIS is an SI-powered fire safety and data analysis dashboard designed for spacecraft, featuring an embedded SI agent named Ember. The system operates in three main phases: Detect, Analyze, and Alert.
First, Ember integrates with spacecraft cameras and uses Edge Computer Vision to monitor live feeds for early signs of fire (smoke, flames, or thermal anomalies). Second, it cross-references any detected anomaly with NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database (BASS, Saffire, FLEX) to understand the material's flammability and fire spread rate in microgravity. Finally, if a threat is confirmed, IGNIS triggers a multi-channel alert: a massive red warning on the dashboard, push notifications to astronaut tablets, and integration with the ISS Caution & Warning (C&W) audible sirens. Astronauts can also interact with Ember via a "Live" chat interface to ask questions, upload photos of anomalies, and receive instant, actionable suppression protocols.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Speed-of-Light Detection: Traditional sensors wait for smoke particles to drift, which doesn't happen in zero-G. IGNIS detects fires visually at "second zero."
  • Zero Latency: By utilizing Ember SI, IGNIS processes data locally on the spacecraft. It continues to function and protect the crew even during communication blackouts with Earth.
  • Actionable Intelligence: Instead of just sounding a siren, the system tells astronauts exactly where the fire is, what class it is, and how to suppress it using historical NASA data.
  • Proactive Mission Planning: The "Compare" feature allows researchers to score materials for future missions, ensuring safer spacecraft design for Moon and Mars bases.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The primary goal of IGNIS is to protect astronaut lives and critical spacecraft infrastructure by transforming over 50 years of passive NASA combustion data into a real-time, life-saving intelligence layer.

  • During Active Missions (Immediate Response): Because smoke does not rise in zero gravity, traditional particle detectors suffer from dangerous delays. By focusing on ISS modules and pressurized rovers, IGNIS spots ignition at "second zero" using computer vision. Delivering instant, context-aware suppression steps directly to astronaut tablets minimizes response times during emergencies in these confined, enclosed habitats.
  • Before Missions Launch (Proactive Prevention): Through our Fit Score comparison engine, engineers and researchers can evaluate material flammability to guide the selection of safer cabin components, fire-resistant spacesuit materials, and hardware for upcoming ISS payloads and rover designs.
  • Deep-Space Autonomy: By running Ember SI locally via Edge computing, spacecraft crews remain protected with zero latency even when communication with Earth is delayed or lost.


4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?
SI & Assistants:

Ember (In-App Assistant): Powered by the Google Gemini API.

Claude (Anthropic): Used for project planning, research, prompt engineering, and structuring JSON datasets.

Replit Agent: Automated full-stack coding, execution, and cloud deployment.

Development, Design & Hosting:

Replit: Cloud environment, code execution, and UI design/prototyping.

Replit Secrets: Secure storage for API keys.

JSON Data Files: Structured data for experiments, alerts, risk/hazard levels, and gravity applications.

External APIs & Data Sources: Google Gemini API, NASA Image and Video Library API, NASA PSI, NTRS, and Spinoff databases.

Presentation: Canva (slides).



5. How is your project creative?

While existing solutions either store NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) datasets as static research archives or rely on basic, single-trigger smoke alarms, IGNIS creatively bridges both worlds into a unified dual-mode ecosystem:

  • Turning Static Archives into an Active "Memory": Instead of merely alerting the crew that a fire exists, Ember cross-references live camera feeds with historical spaceflight experiments (BASS, Saffire, FLEX, ACME) to identify exact fire classes and predict how flames will spread in reduced gravity.
  • Partial-Gravity Predictive Modeling: Rather than treating space as only 0g or 1g, we introduced a Fit Score system that extrapolates flammability risks for partial-gravity environments like the Moon (0.16g) and Mars (0.38g), addressing a major data gap in deep-space mission planning.
  • Multimodal Co-Pilot for High-Stress Situations: Combining computer-vision anomaly bounding boxes with a conversational assistant allows astronauts to upload photos of suspicious smoke or ask urgent questions (e.g., "Where is the nearest extinguisher?") and receive immediate, evidence-backed guidance.

6. What factors did your team consider?

When designing both the IGNIS dashboard and Ember SI architecture, our team accounted for the unique physical, operational, and human factors of spaceflight:

  • Microgravity & Partial-Gravity Physics: Unlike on Earth, flames in microgravity form dim, spherical, low-soot blue spheres, and flammability can actually peak in lunar gravity (0.16g). We trained our logic around visual flame signatures and multi-gravity variables (O2 concentration, cabin pressure, and gravity levels) rather than conventional smoke drift.
  • Communication Latency & Offline Reliability: Deep-space missions experience significant communication lag with Earth. We designed Ember to operate via local Edge SI, ensuring instant anomaly detection and Caution & Warning (C&W) siren activation without relying on ground-control connectivity.
  • Astronaut Cognitive Load Under Stress: During an onboard emergency, crew members cannot sift through complex spreadsheets. We designed a high-contrast, dark-mode HUD interface (#0D1117) that shifts from a detailed research library into a clear, red DANGER alert state with direct location tags (e.g., "Module B, Camera 3") and actionable instructions.
  • False-Alarm Reduction: In a closed spacecraft, false alarms waste valuable crew time and resources. By combining optical/thermal sensor fusion with historical NASA combustion profiles, Ember distinguishes between normal cabin activity (like flashlights or reflections) and true combustion hazards.
